I have enough to diagnose. Here's the chain.

**Why `entire review --findings` shows nothing**

`--findings` reads JSON manifests from `.git/entire-review/manifests/`. You have exactly **one** there — from a May 7 review that ran in `.worktrees/redact`, and the loader's per-worktree filter (`manifest.go:236`) hides it from the main worktree.

**Why your fresh review (12:36–12:52 today) didn't write a new manifest**

`writePostReviewManifest` (`cmd.go:637`) writes a manifest only if it can match each agent run to a session-state file with `Kind == "agent_review"`. The matcher in `manifest.go:104` discards sessions whose `Kind` is anything else — including null. The session JSONs for today's review (`8ad97f8d…` claude-code, `019e0872…` codex) were already cleaned up, but the surviving sessions on disk all show `"kind": null`, and the logs show **zero** "adopted review env" or "adoption skipped" entries during the 12:36–12:52 window. That means the lifecycle hook ran without `ENTIRE_REVIEW_SESSION=1` in its environment — the silent early-return at `lifecycle.go:1042–1043`:

```go
if os.Getenv(review.EnvSession) != "1" {
    return  // no log
}
```

So the env-var handshake `entire review → claude -p → entire <hook>` is broken on your machine: env isn't reaching the hook subprocess. Three branches of `adoptReviewEnv` log on failure (agent mismatch / SHA mismatch / bad JSON); only the "env not set" branch is silent — and that's exactly what you hit. Likely cause is that `claude -p` (the argv `entire review` uses for claude-code, `reviewer.go:32`) is sanitizing or not propagating env to its hook child processes.

**Net effect:** every run silently no-ops the manifest write. `--findings` finds nothing, `--fix` has nothing to resolve.

**Quick way to confirm and unblock**

Run a review with file-level diagnostics, then check if the env actually reached the hook:

```fish
ENTIRE_LOG_LEVEL=debug entire review --agent codex
# in another tab while it runs
grep -E "adopted review|adoption skipped|review manifest" .entire/logs/entire.log | tail
```

Codex is a useful first probe because its launcher (`agent/codex/reviewer.go:39`) and Claude's are structurally identical, so if codex tags the session and claude doesn't, Claude's `-p` mode is the env-stripping culprit. If neither tags the session, the bug is upstream of the agent fork (e.g., the spawn path itself isn't running the AgentReviewer with `cmd.Env` populated).

Either way, the fix likely belongs in #1145's adoption path — adding a more useful "EnvSession unset" debug log would have made this self-diagnosable, and falling back to a checkpoint-id/process-id heuristic in `writePostReviewManifest` when `Kind` matching turns up empty would make the feature degrade gracefully instead of silently producing nothing.

`★ Insight ─────────────────────────────────────`
- The env-var handshake design is elegant when it works: each spawned agent gets its own `ENTIRE_REVIEW_*` env, so multi-tenant correctness is "by construction" with no shared marker file (CLAUDE.md anti-features explicitly bans the older marker-file approach). But it has one fragility this codebase didn't account for: it assumes every agent CLI propagates env to its hook subprocesses unmodified. When a CLI does anything cute with env (whitelist filtering, scrubbing for cache-key stability, `-p` short-circuit paths), the entire feature silently no-ops.
- The "silent failure" in `adoptReviewEnv` line 1042 is exactly the kind of pattern `superpowers:silent-failure-hunter` exists to catch — every other branch logs at WARN, but the most-common-in-practice failure mode logs nothing. That's why this issue is so opaque from the outside: there's no error, no warning, no missing-file message — just an empty `--findings` list with no breadcrumbs.
- A useful debugging shortcut for "env vars not reaching child" bugs in agent CLIs: `strace -f -e trace=execve` (Linux) or `dtruss -f` (macOS) on `entire review` will show every `execve` in the tree along with its argv AND envp, making it obvious where in the parent→agent→hook chain the variable disappears. Cheaper than instrumenting the code.

Three converging causes — none of them caught the bug because each one sits in a blind spot of the next.

**1. The test pyramid never exercised real env propagation.**

Every test stubs out the chain at a different layer:

- `reviewer_test.go:40-62` checks `cmd.Env` on the unexecuted `*exec.Cmd` — verifies the env was set, never runs anything.
- `lifecycle_test.go:1298+` uses `t.Setenv(...)` to put the vars in the *test process's* env, then calls `adoptReviewEnv` directly — verifies the function reads env correctly, never goes through a subprocess.
- `integration_test/review_test.go:41-50` builds a synthetic `reviewEnv` slice and hands it to `SimulateUserPromptSubmitWithReviewEnvVars` — verifies the adoption pipeline if the env is present, never tests that it gets there.
- The Vogon canary (`e2e/vogon/`) doesn't cover the `--findings`/`--fix`/footer code path at all.
- Real-agent E2E tests are gated behind `mise run test:e2e` and aren't part of `test:ci`, so they don't block merges.

The PR's verification block (`go test ./cmd/entire/cli/review ./cmd/entire/cli ./cmd/entire/cli/settings`) ran exactly these green-but-blind tests. So "all tests pass" gave full confidence in a propagation chain whose middle link was never executed.

**2. The design assumed a property that doesn't always hold.**

`AppendReviewEnv` (`env.go:94`) and `adoptReviewEnv` (`lifecycle.go:1037`) form a contract: parent sets env on agent process, agent inherits, agent's hook subprocess inherits transitively. That works *if* the agent CLI passes its own env to hook subprocesses verbatim. Claude Code in `-p` (one-shot) mode is the most likely violator — `claude -p` is the argv `entire review` uses for claude-code (`reviewer.go:32`), and `-p` mode has historically had different lifecycle semantics than interactive mode. Other launchable agents (codex, gemini-cli) plausibly behave the same way or differently; the design treated them all uniformly. The CLAUDE.md anti-features section even brags about ditching the older marker-file approach in favor of "multi-tenant correctness by construction" — that's correct *given* the propagation assumption, but the assumption itself was never validated.

**3. The failure mode collapses three signals into one silent return.**

`lifecycle.go:1042-1043`:

```go
if os.Getenv(review.EnvSession) != "1" {
    return  // no log
}
```

This branch fires for two semantically different cases:
- **Normal session** — silence is correct (don't spam logs for every non-review turn).
- **Review session whose env was stripped** — silence hides the bug.

The hook can't distinguish them from inside, because the only signal that "this *should* be a review" is the env var that just went missing. So the bug presents identically to normal operation: no error, no warning, no missing-file message. Then three downstream features (manifest persistence, `--findings`, end-of-run footer) all gate on the same `Kind == "agent_review"` check at `manifest.go:104`, so a single silent miss kills them as a unit.

**Net causal story:** PR #1145 replaced a marker-file design (which would have shown a stale or missing file diagnostically) with an env-var design (which fails invisibly when env is stripped); the test suite never executed the propagation chain end-to-end; the failure handler treats "env missing" as the no-op default; and three user-visible features were factored to share that single silently-failing check. Each of those choices is locally reasonable; together they produce a feature that ships green and silently no-ops in production.

`★ Insight ─────────────────────────────────────`
- The deeper lesson is about **test coverage at the boundary you actually care about**. The PR has unit tests on both *sides* of the env handshake (sender sets env correctly; receiver reads env correctly) but no test of the wire between them. This is a recurring pattern in subprocess-mediated features — and the only reliable defense is a test that actually forks the real CLI and inspects the resulting subprocess env (e.g., a tiny "echo my env" agent in `e2e/vogon/` that prints `ENTIRE_REVIEW_*` to stderr, which the test scrapes). A 15-line addition to the canary would have caught this on the merging PR.
- The marker-file → env-var migration was sold as a fix for a multi-tenant correctness problem (concurrent worktrees racing on a shared file). But the new design just trades one class of bugs for another: marker files have visible, debuggable state; env vars have invisible, ephemeral state that vanishes the moment a subprocess fork doesn't cooperate. Both have legitimate failure modes — the question is which failure mode you can *detect*. A hybrid (env-var primary, marker-file fallback at agent-spawn time so the hook can probe both) is uglier but bulletproof, and would have given today's symptom an immediately legible diagnosis.
- Worth noting that this codebase already has a `superpowers:silent-failure-hunter` agent specifically calibrated to flag exactly this `if cond { return }` pattern in code review. If it had been run against #1145's diff at PR time, the silent return at `lifecycle.go:1042` is exactly the kind of construct it would have surfaced — combined with the matcher's silent skip at `manifest.go:104` and the manifest write's silent early returns at `cmd.go:645/653`, that's *four* silent failure points stacked in a row, none of which log anything an operator can grep for. Running the silent-failure-hunter on review-related diffs going forward would catch the next instance of this class.
`─────────────────────────────────────────────────`

**The May 7 manifest was written 2 hours BEFORE #1145 merged to main** (manifest at 19:55 UTC; merge at 21:47 UTC). Which means: the user wrote it from a checkout of the feature branch in `.worktrees/redact`, almost certainly while testing the PR. That run worked. Today's run on main, with the same code (now merged), didn't. So the code paths are identical — what changed is the *runtime environment* the review is running inside.

Look at this log line from today's review:

```
"session_id":"6a33efd5-..."   ← ambient logging context
"event":"SessionStart"
"session_id":"8ad97f8d-..."   ← the actual review session
```

The session_id appears twice. The outer one (`6a33efd5`) is your daytime ambient claude-code session — running since 11:03 today. The inner one (`8ad97f8d`) is the review. So `entire review` wasn't run from a fresh terminal — it was run from *inside* an outer claude session, almost certainly via the Bash tool.

That changes the env-propagation chain meaningfully:

```
fresh terminal:   fish → entire review → claude -p  → entire <hook>
                                          ↑ env set here, inherited cleanly

via outer claude: outer-claude → Bash tool → entire review → claude -p → entire <hook>
                                  ↑ env may be filtered/sanitized here ↑ may inherit a DIFFERENT outer env
```

What "new terminal" actually rules out

Your old shell had something in its environment that the new one didn't. Two candidates account for almost all "works in fresh shell" cases:

1. **Stale `ENTIRE_REVIEW_*` from a prior aborted run** — if you ever exported these manually for debugging, or a previous `entire review` left them set in your shell (it shouldn't, but a crashed parent could), `os.Environ()` in the new run picks them up. `AppendReviewEnv` (env.go:97-101) tries to defend against this by stripping pre-existing `ENTIRE_REVIEW_*` keys before re-adding them, so this path *should* be safe — but only for those specific keys.

2. **Ambient state from a parent agent process** — your old terminal was inside or downstream of an active claude-code session (likely `6a33efd5`, which the logs show was alive all day). When that session shells out, it injects its own `CLAUDE_*` markers and may filter or replace env. If anything in that chain dropped or rewrote a var the spawn path needed (PATH, HOME, GIT_*), `paths.WorktreeRoot(ctx)` or `git rev-parse HEAD` inside `entire review` would resolve differently than they do in your new terminal — and `cfg.StartingSHA` would end up empty or wrong, blowing the SHA check at `lifecycle.go:1052` silently.

You can identify which one by running this in your *old* terminal (don't open a new one first):

```fish
env | grep -E '^(ENTIRE_|CLAUDE_|GIT_|PATH=|HOME=|PWD=)' | sort
```

Compare to the same command in a fresh terminal. The diff is the proximate cause.

Why this needs fixing regardless

The bug isn't "stale env in shell" — that's a user-state issue. The bug is that **the failure mode is invisible**. Three small fixes would make this self-diagnosing instead of "open an issue and pray someone reproduces it":

1. **lifecycle.go:1042** — replace the silent return with a debug log: `logging.Debug(ctx, "review env adoption skipped: ENTIRE_REVIEW_SESSION not set", ...)`. Five lines. Today's whole hour-long debugging session collapses to one grep.

2. **cmd.go:653** — when `manifest.Sources == 0`, print a *user-visible* warning to stderr (not just debug log): `"warning: review completed but session was not tagged as a review; --findings will not see this run. Run with ENTIRE_LOG_LEVEL=debug to diagnose."` That single line means the next user hits the same bug and can self-help instead of opening "feature doesn't work" with no logs.

3. **`AppendReviewEnv` is too narrow** — it strips stale `ENTIRE_REVIEW_*` but doesn't probe whether the env actually arrives at the hook. A simple defense: have `entire review` write a sentinel file at `<git-common-dir>/entire-review/.handshake-<run-id>` containing `{run_id, starting_sha, agent}`, set `ENTIRE_REVIEW_RUN=<run-id>` on the spawned agent, and at hook time look up the sentinel by run-id env var. If the env var arrived → use the env path. If not → fall back to "look for any sentinel younger than this hook's SessionStart that names this agent." Belt-and-suspenders, costs ~30 lines, and the marker file is debuggable when env propagation fails (you can `cat` it and see exactly what the parent set).

The CLAUDE.md anti-features list explicitly bans the `PendingReviewMarker` for launchable agents because the env-var design "makes it unnecessary." That was true on a clean process tree. It's not true under nested agent invocations. The marker isn't a regression — it's a fallback for when the elegant primary path can't deliver.

- "Works in a fresh terminal" is a load-bearing diagnostic clue for env-propagation bugs, but it's also a tell that the feature has an undeclared precondition: *the ambient environment must be clean*. Features should declare their preconditions in code (validate, fail loudly) or eliminate the dependency on them. Silently degrading when a precondition isn't met is the worst outcome — the feature appears to run, costs full agent tokens, and produces nothing.
- The fact that #1145's tests all pass but the feature breaks under realistic invocation is a useful generalization: when a feature's contract spans process boundaries, *unit tests on either side of the boundary are insufficient by construction* — only end-to-end tests that actually fork the boundary can verify it. The CLAUDE.md anti-features section is sound design advice for the happy path; it's wrong about the unhappy path.

Many codebases accumulate warnings that print on every invocation "just in case," and users learn to tune them out. A warning that only fires when the stated invariant has actually been violated retains its signal value. Users who never hit the bug never see the warning; users who hit it learn from it.

The user-visible warning answers "did my run work?" — which is what users care about. The debug log answers "*why* didn't it work?" — which is what the next bug-fixing engineer needs. PR descriptions for observability fixes should make that distinction explicit so reviewers don't ask "why are we logging the same thing twice?" — they're not, they're capturing different facts for different readers.
